# Pronouncing Kyūshū: a guide for the curious

Saying **Kyūshū** aloud is harder than reading it on a screen, and more rewarding. The restored spelling is a compressed pronunciation guide: every accent and macron is an instruction. This post unpacks those instructions — the reconstructed sound, the phoneme-by-phoneme record, the kindred forms in neighboring languages — and then zooms out to the full record around the name: its Japanese characters writing, its mythology, its cult, and its modern life as a Unicode domain. Whether you arrive as a linguist, a reader of myth, or a domainer, you will leave able to say the name the way the evidence suggests it was said — and able to type it the way it was written.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Kyūshū
- **ASCII form:** kyushu
- **Meaning:** "'Nine provinces' (九州)"
- **Domain of influence:** South, Volcanoes, Origins
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 九州 (Japanese characters)
- **Live domain:** kyūshū.com

## Overview

**Kyūshū** (*kyushu*) — The Nine Provinces — belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "South, Volcanoes, Origins". The name means "'Nine provinces' (九州)".

Kyūshū is Japan's front door: the island facing Korea and China across the narrowest straits, where the continent's rice, Buddhism, and iron first arrived — and where the Mongol fleets, the Portuguese traders, and the Jesuit fathers all made their landfall. The gateway of Japan has always stood open on this shore, even when the country tried to shut it.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Kyūshū** and serves its temple at [kyūshū.com](https://xn--kysh-w7ac.com). The restoration preserves the long ū vowels — distinctive features the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *kyushu* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Kyūshū** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "'Nine provinces' (九州)".

The ASCII form *kyushu* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Kyūshū** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves the long ū vowels — distinctive features the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **k** → **K** — Same letter
- **y** → **y** — Same letter
- **u** → **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **s** → **s** — Same letter
- **h** → **h** — Same letter
- **u** → **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel

The project holds the domain **kyūshū.com** (xn--kysh-w7ac.com) as the canonical home of this name.

## The Original Script

The original script for this japanese name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.

The form **Kyūshū** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

Written 九州: kyū (nine) plus shū (province). The island's ancient name 筑紫 (Tsukushi) is preserved in the Kojiki's island-birth account — "Kyūshū" is the administrative name that replaced the mythic one and quietly kept the older island's memory of division.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/kjɯː.ɕɯː/** — Japanese (Hepburn).

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: KYOO-shoo, with the compressed ky- onset and long vowels.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Japanese** — 九州
- **Ancient name** — Tsukushi
- **Owned form** — Kyūshū

Kyūshū 九州 — "Nine Provinces" — carries the long ū in both syllables, both preserved in the restoration. The name remembers the island's ancient division into nine provinces; its older name, Tsukushi, appears in the earliest chronicles as the gateway of the gods' descent. Both syllables are long in kana (きゅうしゅう); the two macrons of the restoration are the two doubled vowels.

## Mythology

Kyūshū claims the mythology of beginnings: the chronicles land the sun goddess's grandson on its peaks, and its storms wrote themselves into the national soul.

### Ninigi on Takachiho (The Descent)

The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki bring the heavenly grandson Ninigi down to earth on the peak of Takachiho — placed by tradition in Kyūshū's mountains — where he marries the blossom-princess Konohanasakuya-hime. She proves her divine conception by setting fire to the birthing hut and delivering three sons amid the flames; their line leads to Jimmu, the first emperor. The imperial charter myth is, geographically, a Kyūshū story.

### The Divine Wind (The Storm)

Twice the Mongol-Chinese fleets of Kublai Khan reached Kyūshū — 1274 and 1281, the second numbering thousands of ships — and twice, after hard fighting on the Hakata beaches, typhoons destroyed the armadas. The shrines had prayed for deliverance, and the nation named the storm kamikaze, "divine wind": weather as providence, and the coast of Hakata Bay as the sacrificial altar of the world's largest seaborne invasions.

### The Kirishitan Century (The Hidden Faith)

Francis Xavier landed at Kagoshima in 1549; within decades Kyūshū had a quarter-million Christians, daimyō baptized with their domains, and seminaries at Arima and Azuchi. Then came the turn: persecution, crucifixions at Nagasaki, the Shimabara-Amakusa rising of 1637 — and 250 years of hidden Christians keeping Latin prayers in corrupted Japanese, baptizing in secret, venerating statues of Kannon as Maria. Their revelation in 1865, when farmers of Urakami knelt before a French priest, stunned the mission world.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Kyūshū concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The kamikaze banner** — The storm as protector — weather enlisted in the national myth
- **The Aso caldera** — One of the world's great volcanic craters — the island's fiery heart
- **The Dejima fan** — The tiny artificial island that carried Europe into Japan for 200 years

## Archaeology & Evidence

Yoshinogari, in Saga, is East Asia's great Yayoi site: a moated, towered settlement of two thousand years ago, with mass jar-burials and bronze-weapon caches — the archaeological face of the Wa people whom Chinese chronicles describe. The underwater archaeology of Takashima's Mongol wrecks — anchor stones, bombs, and hulls preserved in Imari Bay — has recovered the kamikaze fleets themselves. The hidden Christian sites of the Amakusa islands and Nagasaki's Ōura Cathedral (1864, built for the returned faith) are UNESCO-listed as the "Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region."

## Realm & Domain

Kyūshū is Japan's front door: the island facing Korea and China across the narrowest straits, where the continent's rice, Buddhism, and iron first arrived — and where the Mongol fleets, the Portuguese traders, and the Jesuit fathers all made their landfall. The gateway of Japan has always stood open on this shore, even when the country tried to shut it.

### The Straits

Tsushima and Korea are a day's sail — Asia has always been closer here than Tōkyō.

### The Kamikaze

The "divine wind" typhoons of 1274 and 1281 that shattered two Mongol invasion fleets off this coast.

### Nagasaki

The one window kept open in the closed country: two centuries of Dutch and Chinese trade through a single fan-shaped island.

### The Christian Century

Xavier's 1549 landing, a quarter-million converts, the Shimabara rising, and the hidden Christians' 250-year secret.

## Across Cultures

Kyūshū is Japan's syncretic laboratory: Korean potters founding Arita porcelain, Chinese merchant quarters at Nagasaki, Portuguese words entering the language (pan, tempura, kappa), Dutch learning (Rangaku) flowing through Dejima into Japanese science — anatomy, astronomy, and artillery smuggled in translation. The island's cuisine, dialects, and crafts all carry the gateway's mark: everything Japanese that came from outside came here first.

Within the Japanese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[fujin|Fūjin]], [[hokkaido|Hokkaidō]], [[honshu|Honshū]], [[jizo|Jizō]], [[kobe|Kōbe]], and [[kyoto|Kyōto]].

## Cultural Legacy

The kamikaze of 1281 gave the 20th century its most terrible word; Nagasaki's 1945 atomic bombing made the island a symbol of the nuclear age's cost, and its peace park one of the world's pilgrimage sites of memory. Arita and Imari porcelain conquered European markets and imitators for three centuries. Today the island's universities and semiconductor fabs continue the oldest pattern: the gateway as Japan's technology shore.

## A Meditation

Kyūshū is the island that opens. Rice, writing, Buddhism, gunpowder, Christianity, Western science — all knocked on this shore, and Japan answered differently each time: embrace, storm, secrecy, translation. It asks the gateway's question, which is every border's question: what do you let in — and what does the letting-in make of you?

The gateway's pattern persists in silicon: the island that took in rice, iron, scripture, and surgery now takes in the semiconductor supply chain, and Kumamoto's fabs are Tsukushi's old role in new matter. Every borderland knows its double exposure — first to the gift, first to the invasion — and Kyūshū's answer has been constant for two thousand years: translate everything, fear nothing twice, and keep the door's hinges oiled.

And the island's two great memories — the divine wind and the atomic one — face each other across eight centuries: the storm that saved and the bomb that burned, both arriving from the same sky over the same coast. Kyūshū carries them without resolving them, which is the gateway's last lesson: the shore that opens to the world must be ready for everything the world brings, the sutra and the cannonball, the virus and the vaccine, the answer arriving, as always, by sea.

The straits have not moved; the gateway still opens each morning to the same west. What changes is only the cargo — sutras once, silicon now — and the island's ancient readiness to receive it, translate it, and make it Japanese.

## The Unicode Restoration

Kyūshū is classified as **Tier 1**: the restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses. The ASCII fallback *kyushu* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 6 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 2: 2 marks of length (ū, ū). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **kyūshū.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode form as xn--kysh-w7ac.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Kyūshū; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Japanese characters can now be typed into any browser on earth.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does Kyūshū mean?** The traditional gloss is "'Nine provinces' (九州)."

**Which tradition does Kyūshū belong to?** Kyūshū is catalogued in the Japanese pantheon of the PuniCodex lexicon.

**Why is Kyūshū classified as Tier 1?** Because the restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses — and the marks in the restored spelling preserve exactly that evidence.

**Is Kyūshū a working domain?** Yes — kyūshū.com resolves today and routes to this temple.

**What is the punycode for kyūshū.com?** The DNS encoding is xn--kysh-w7ac.com; browsers perform the translation automatically, so visitors only ever see the restored name.

**Can I use Kyūshū in a normal browser?** Yes. The DNS resolves the punycode form automatically, and the type tool on this site converts kyushu to Kyūshū for copying and pasting.

**Where does the scholarly information come from?** The entry is built from lexica, inscriptional evidence, and reviewed scholarly sources listed in the Scholarly Edition. Every claim is traceable to a canonical source.

## Why This Restoration Matters

Pronunciation turns out to be the heart of the matter. The marks in **Kyūshū** are instructions for the voice, and a web that strips them is a web that mispronounces the past at scale. The restoration hands the instructions back: say it as the evidence suggests, type it as the tradition wrote it, and let the punycode machinery do the quiet translation in between. That is all the PuniCodex project asks of the infrastructure — and everything it asks of you, the reader, is to use the whole name.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Kyūshū**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *kyushu* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 6 characters, 4 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **k** stays as it is — Same letter.

The **y** stays as it is — Same letter.

The **u** becomes **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel.

The **s** stays as it is — Same letter.

The **h** stays as it is — Same letter.

The **u** becomes **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.

## Kyūshū in Its Tradition

**Kyūshū** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is counted among 45 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — South, Volcanoes, Origins — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Kyūshū**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Kyūshū** is one such vote.
